t: Rearrange Spaces Between Words: Count, Divide, Rebuild
o:
## Understanding the problem

You are handed a string made only of lowercase words and spaces, and you may rearrange **only the spaces**: words keep their relative order, every adjacent pair of words must be separated by the same number of spaces, that number must be maximized, and leftovers go to the very end. The output always has exactly the same length as the input.

**Example 1:** `"  this   is  a sentence "` contains 9 spaces and 4 words. There are 3 gaps between 4 words, and floor(9 / 3) = 3 spaces fit in each gap with no remainder, so the answer is `"this   is   a   sentence"`.

**Example 2:** `" practice   makes   perfect"` contains 7 spaces and 3 words: floor(7 / 2) = 3 spaces per gap plus 1 extra, which is appended to the end, giving `"practice   makes   perfect "`.

Constraints are tiny (length at most 100), so efficiency is irrelevant; correctness hinges on bookkeeping - counting spaces, extracting words, and rebuilding with integer division.
k: The output is a permutation of the input's characters, so everything reduces to two numbers: the total space count and the word count.
There are (words - 1) gaps; integer division of spaces by that gives the per-gap count, and the remainder goes to the end.
Single-word inputs are the main edge case: zero gaps exist, so every space trails behind the one word.

a.i: Let the language do the tokenizing: count the spaces, split the text on whitespace discarding empty tokens, then rebuild. The only care point is the degenerate case of one word, where there are no gaps at all and every space lands at the end.
s: Count the space characters in text.
Split text into words, dropping empty tokens produced by consecutive or leading/trailing spaces.
If there is exactly one word, return it followed by all spaces.
Otherwise divide spaces by (words - 1): the quotient separates adjacent words, the remainder is appended.
a.t: O(n) - each character is examined a constant number of times across counting, splitting, and joining.
a.sp: O(n) - the word list and result buffer hold the whole text.

a.i: Parse by hand instead of relying on split/regex: walk the string once, tallying spaces and accumulating letters into the current word. This is the version you write when library helpers are off-limits, and it makes the mechanics explicit: flush a word whenever a space follows letters, then flush once more after the loop ends.
s: Scan character by character, counting spaces.
Accumulate letters; when a space follows letters, close out the current word.
Flush any pending word after the scan finishes.
Distribute spaces with divmod(spaces, words - 1) exactly as before and build the output.
a.t: O(n) - one scan plus linear output construction.
a.sp: O(n) - for the extracted words and the result.

w:
Go with Approach 1 in an interview - it is shorter and harder to get wrong - and mention you can drop to a manual scan if built-ins are off-limits.

**Pitfalls.** Forgetting the one-word case (division by zero on words - 1); miscounting gaps as words instead of words - 1; dropping or inventing spaces so the output length no longer equals text.length.

**Follow-ups.** Treating tabs/newlines as separators too, streaming input where words arrive one at a time, or capping the number of spaces allowed per gap.
